data.title: Slavic hillforts in Germany – the Polabian and Baltic Slavs
data.excerpt: From the end of the 6th to the middle of the 13th century the east, north and north-west of present-day Germany were held by West Slavic tribes — the Lusatians, the Liutizi, the Obotrites, the Pomeranians and the Rani. Nine of their hillforts are presented here, from Gross Raden and Raddusch through Arkona and Köpenick to Stargrad, several of them rebuilt today as open-air museums.
data.metaTitle: Slavic hillforts in Germany – the Polabian and Baltic Slavs
data.metaDescription: From the 6th to the 13th century West Slavic tribes held eastern and northern Germany. A tour of nine of their hillforts, from Gross Raden to Stargrad.

keyFacts.label: Gross Raden
keyFacts.value: Hillfort and sanctuary of the Warnower by Lake Binnensee, a circular timber-and-earth rampart 50 m in diameter; today an open-air museum (reconstructed in 1987)

keyFacts.label: Raddusch
keyFacts.value: An oval hillfort of the Lusatians between Lübbenau and Cottbus, today reconstructed as it looked 1,000 years ago

keyFacts.label: Arkona
keyFacts.value: The best-known Slavic hillfort in Germany, on the island of Rujana (Rügen), seat of the cult of Svantovít

keyFacts.label: Torgelow
keyFacts.value: A reconstructed Slavic village of the 9th–10th centuries in Ukranenland, with replicas of the ships Svarog (1997) and Svantovit (1998)

keyFacts.label: Köpenick
keyFacts.value: A castle island in Berlin, centre of the Sprevani tribe; Prince Jaxa of Köpenick defeated Albrecht the Bear in 1157, the hillfort was taken by 1178 at the latest

keyFacts.label: Spandau
keyFacts.value: Hillfort of the Hevelli at the mouth of the Spree, flourishing from the end of the 10th to the middle of the 12th century, ended after its capture by Albrecht the Bear (1157)

keyFacts.label: Behren-Lübchin
keyFacts.value: An island hillfort of the Circipani mentioned by Saxo Grammaticus (1171), one of the last to resist German and Christian expansion

keyFacts.label: Stargrad (Oldenburg)
keyFacts.value: Chief town of the Wagri tribe, seat of the prince and a sanctuary; today reconstructed at the Oldenburger Wallmuseum

timeline.title: Arrival of the West Slavic tribes
timeline.description: The Lusatians, the Liutizi, the Obotrites, the Pomeranians and the Rani settled the east, north and north-west of present-day Germany after the departure of the Germanic tribes.

timeline.title: Foundation of the Raddusch hillfort
timeline.description: An oval hillfort on the shore of the Bischdorf lake in Lower Lusatia, with walls 10 m thick and two tunnel gateways.

timeline.title: The earlier phase of the Gross Raden hillfort
timeline.description: An important hillfort and sanctuary of the Warnower tribe on the peninsula by Lake Binnensee; destroyed a few decades later.

timeline.title: Destruction of the occupation at Gross Raden
timeline.description: The settlement and the sanctuary were destroyed by fire; the cause is not documented by written sources. It was quickly rebuilt, with larger houses and the sanctuary moved.

timeline.title: Successive rebuildings of the Raddusch hillfort
timeline.description: The fortifications were renovated twice, the interior gradually shrinking from 35–36 m to 28 m in diameter.

timeline.title: Siege of Brandenburg an der Havel
timeline.description: The seat hillfort of the Hevellian princes was besieged by the German king Henry I.

timeline.title: Conquest of Lusatia by Margrave Gero
timeline.description: It meant the end of the Raddusch hillfort, which was left abandoned and gradually fell into decay.

timeline.title: Final abandonment of Gross Raden
timeline.description: The settlement was destroyed for a second time and finally abandoned, probably in connection with the campaign of Otto III against the Mecklenburg Slavs in 995.

timeline.title: Demise of the Brandenburg hillfort
timeline.description: After the death of Prince Pribislav-Henry (1150) the hillfort passed to Albrecht the Bear (definitively in 1157); in 1165 a Christian cathedral was built on its site.

timeline.title: Archaeological excavation at Raddusch
timeline.description: It demonstrated occupation of the site as early as the end of the Bronze Age and in the Migration Period; the hillfort has now been reconstructed in its Slavic form.

children.text: As modern history testifies, from roughly the end of the 6th to the middle of the 13th century AD the east, north and north-west of present-day Germany were inhabited by large groups of West Slavic tribes — the Lusatians (Lusatian Sorbs), the Liutizi, the Obotrites, the Pomeranians and the Rani — and by further tribes which are today called the Polabian or the Baltic Slavs. In the second half of the 6th century these tribes replaced the Germanic tribes of the Langobards, the Rugii, the Lugii, the Chizobradi, the Varini, the Veledi and others, who had already lived here in antiquity but later abandoned their territories and moved elsewhere.

From the 6th century onwards the Slavs occupied an extensive territory from the mouth of the Elbe and its tributary the Saale in the west as far as the Oder in the east, and from the Ore Mountains (on the border with the Czech Republic) in the south to the Baltic Sea in the north. The land of the Polabian Slavs thus took up at least a third of the present-day German state. The Polabian Slavs were grouped in three tribal confederations: the Lusatian Sorbs, the Liutizi (Veleti) and the Obotrites (Abodrites, Rarogi or Reregi). Related to them were also the Pomeranian tribes living on the southern shore of the Baltic Sea, roughly from the mouth of the Oder to the mouth of the Vistula and, in the south, as far as the river Noteć on the border with the Polish tribes.

The fact that Slavic peoples lived in the territory of Germany in times long past is attested by the many toponyms they left behind (from topos — “place” — and onom — “name, designation”, a noun denoting the name of a geographical feature). For example:
Berlin
, Schwerin, Witzin, Devín, Alt Teterin, Karpin. The ending “-in” in Slavic toponyms carries the stress.
Lausitz (Lužice), Chemnitz, Dobranitz (Dobrancy), Doberschütz (Dobrosicy), Doberschau (Dobruša).
Lübow, Teterow, Güstrow, Lütow, Golzow, Mirow, Burow.
Lübbenau, Schandau, Torgau.

blocks.text: ... The realm of the Slavs is ten times greater than our Saxony, if one counts in with it the Bohemians and the Poles dwelling on this side of the Oder, who differ in no way from the inhabitants of the Slavic realm either in appearance or in speech ... Of the Slavic peoples there are many. The greatest of them are the Wagri to the west, dwelling on the border with the Transalbingians. Their city, which lies by the sea, is Oldenburg (Stargrad). Next after them follow the Abodrites, who are now called Reregi, and their city Magnopolis (Velehrad). To the east of us (of Hamburg) dwell the Polabi (Polabians), whose city is called Racesburg (Ratibor). Beyond them are the Lingones (Glinjani) and the Warnabi. Then follow the Chizzini and the Circipani, who are separated from the Tholenzi and the Redarii by the river Peene and the city of Demmin. There lies the boundary of the diocese of Hamburg. The Chizzini and the Circipani dwell to the north of the river Peene, the Tholenzi and the Redarii to the south. These four peoples are, by reason of their valour, called Wilzi or Liutizi. There are also other Slavic tribes which dwell between the Elbe and the Oder.
blocks.source: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (Deeds of the Bishops of the Church of Hamburg), c. 1066

children.text: In Germany there are several open-air archaeological museums presenting reconstructed Slavic hillforts, large settlements and villages of the 7th–12th centuries. Hillforts were usually founded — as in the territory of present-day Slovakia — at a strategic spot, on a rise, on a high river bank or beside a river ford. Another typical location was an island in a lake linked to the shore by a bridge. Let us therefore mention just a few of the most interesting Slavic hillforts from the territory of Germany.
1. Gross Raden

Gross Raden was a large hillfort and at the same time an important sanctuary of the Slavic tribe of the Warnower. The hillfort, which some 1,000 years ago stood on a peninsula, was reconstructed in 1987 and today holds one of the finest open-air archaeological museums in Europe. The museum lies a few kilometres north of the town of Sternberg and about 1 km north-east of the present-day village of Gross Raden, directly on the northern arm of Lake Binnensee. On the peninsula a massive circular timber-and-earth rampart 50 metres in diameter can be made out from a distance. Extensive excavations were carried out here between 1973 and 1980, during which the remains of a Slavic hillfort of the 9th and 10th centuries were revealed. It turned out that the construction of the hillfort had two main phases. The earlier hillfort was built in the second half of the 9th century and was destroyed a few decades later. The second phase was built shortly afterwards. The hillfort itself stood on an island joined by a bridge to the settlement on the peninsula, which at that time was much smaller than it is today. The peninsula was enclosed only by a ditch 4.5 m wide and a single row of palisades. The only access to the hillfort was along the bridge just mentioned.

In the first decades the occupation probably consisted of about 40 houses built close to one another. The houses had an area of about 4 × 5 m. Judging by the surviving remains of characteristic structural elements, the walls of a house were about two metres high and consisted of beams set vertically into the ground at regular intervals and joined to one another by wattle. A clay plaster was applied to the wattle.

On the open ground of the south-eastern part of the peninsula stood a single-room hall (7 × 11 m) linked by a narrow path lined with stelae to the wooden road that ran through the hillfort. Its rectangular plan was slightly bowed on the shorter sides, which were fitted with entrances. The walls were formed by a double row of pointed planks set into the ground, of which the inner row was load-bearing and the outer decorative. In the rounded, or rather lozenge-pointed, carved heads at their upper ends we can make out hints of male and female figures. The interior of the temple was damaged by a later ditch, so that no traces have survived of the position of any idol. The inventory, however, included 6 horse skulls, 2 iron spears, a wooden shield and bowls on small feet. A cattle skull was hung above the door of the temple.

A short distance from the houses a working area was found, containing clay bread ovens and remains of grain. In the open areas between the buildings and the palisade there were probably regular markets and assemblies. Around the year 900 the occupation was completely destroyed, as indicated by clear signs of fire, chiefly on the palisade and the gateway. Not even the sanctuary was spared. Since we have no written sources from this period about armed conflicts in the area, the cause of the catastrophe remains unknown. The occupation was then quickly renewed and the features rebuilt, but laid out so that the houses this time stood in blocks. The houses were also markedly larger than the earlier ones. The sanctuary was moved to the island and built in a way already different from the original one. For its defence a timber-and-earth rampart 10 m high with an internal diameter of 25 m was erected. This created a well-fortified hillfort on the island. As has already been mentioned, the hillfort was entered along the bridge, and roughly halfway along it there was a control point – a kind of gatehouse. At the end of the 10th century the settlement was finally abandoned after being destroyed for a second time. Again, the reasons are not clear, but it may have been connected with the campaign of Otto III against the Mecklenburg Slavs in 995.

children.text: 2. Raddusch

Another important Slavic hillfort that has been reconstructed in Germany is Raddusch. The hillfort lies by the Bischdorf lake in Lower Lusatia, between the towns of Lübbenau and Cottbus, about 176 km north of Liberec. In the past the area was settled by the Slavic tribe of the Lusatians, who left behind a great number of Slavic place names; the ethnic minority of the Lusatian Sorbs, who are their direct descendants, still lives in the area.

Construction of the hillfort began on the lake shore around 880. The hillfort was oval in shape, its walls were 10 m thick and the interior of the hillfort measured 35 to 36 metres in diameter. The hillfort had two tunnel gateways, placed almost exactly on opposite sides, and it was surrounded by a moat. In 925 the hillfort was renovated, the walls being widened so that the interior shrank to 31 metres. The hillfort underwent a further rebuilding around 950 and the interior shrank again – this time to 28 metres in diameter. In 963 the region of Lusatia was conquered by the German margrave Gero, which also meant the end of the Raddusch hillfort; it was left abandoned and gradually decayed and fell apart. Until 1984 agricultural work was carried out on the site of the hillfort, which considerably disturbed its remains. In the end all that was left of it was a circular mound about 3 m high and some 85 m in diameter. From 1984 to 1989 the hillfort was archaeologically investigated, and it was established that occupation of the hillfort existed on the same spot as early as the end of the Bronze Age and also in the Migration Period.

children.text: Today — as can be seen well in the photographs — the hillfort has been reconstructed once again in the form it had in the Slavic period 1,000 years ago. Inside the hillfort there are reconstructed rooms, an exhibition area, a small shop and social rooms where various lectures and other educational activities on history can be held. An educational trail runs around the hillfort, taking visitors back to a long-vanished age when the hillfort was enjoying its heyday.
3. Arkona
Of course, we cannot leave out the best-known hillfort in Germany either —
Arkona
, situated on the island of Rujana (Rügen), about which I write elsewhere. I do, however, bring a few interesting pictures relating to Arkona, which a friend from Germany sent me.
4. Torgelow
The land once belonging to the Ukrani is today called Uckermark in Germany. In
Ukranenland
Torgelow

a Slavic village of the 9th–10th centuries has been reconstructed to its original extent following archaeological survey. On a visit to this museum you can see with your own eyes what the ships of the Slavic seafarers who ruled the Baltic Sea at that time looked like, become acquainted with the life of Slavic farmers and craftsmen of the period, watch the work of a bronze caster, a potter, a smith and brewers, listen to medieval music and taste the food of the time. Visitors to the museum can also buy pickled vegetables and jams, taste freshly brewed beer and learn to work with clay. At the museum's landing stage you can see the barque “Svarog” — the first reconstructed Slavic ship in Germany, built on the basis of archaeological finds on the island of Rujana in the town of Ralswiek. This type of ship is dated to 900 years ago. The reconstruction was completed in 1997. And also the barque “Svantovit” — a reconstruction of a Polish ship found during excavations in the small town of Lebafelde, also known as Charbrow (built around 1100), reconstructed in 1998.

children.text: 5. Köpenick

In the south-eastern part of Berlin lies the so-called Köpenick castle island, which stands in the river Dahme just before its confluence with the Spree. In the Slavic period a hillfort existed here, apparently from as early as the 7th century, and several further fortified sites were built in its vicinity. These hillforts were very often attacked by the enemy and partly destroyed. This happened above all in the 10th century, when the Germans attempted to colonise the territories inhabited by the Slavs. In 1100 the hillfort was rebuilt and became the centre of the Slavic tribe of the Sprevani. The name of the prince who resided at the hillfort has also been recorded — “Jaxa of Köpenick”, who in 1157 defeated Albrecht the Bear in a decisive battle at Brandenburg on the river Havel. “Jaxa” then withdrew back to Köpenick. How much longer the hillfort resisted German pressure within their “Ostkolonisierung” is no longer known. By 1178 at the latest, however, the hillfort was taken by the Germans. Today almost no visible traces of the hillfort remain, but archaeological excavation has revealed a fairly detailed plan of the hillfort, from which a clear idea of its appearance in the Slavic period can be formed.
6. Spandau

The beginnings of the town of Spandau are to be found about a kilometre south of the present-day town, where an important Slavic hillfort stood 1,000 years ago. In the Early Middle Ages the area around the mouth of the Spree formed several islands, and on one of them, south of the river mouth, the Slavic tribe of the Hevelli already lived in the 7th century, controlling the whole area at that time. At the beginning of the 8th century the Hevelli built an important hillfort here, which experienced its greatest flowering from the end of the 10th to the middle of the 12th century. At that time the hillfort profited greatly from its favourable position on an old trade route. The golden age of the hillfort ended when the area was conquered by Albrecht the Bear in 1157. Today almost nothing remains of the hillfort, but during the excavations various objects were found, such as wicker baskets, needles, awls, handles, containers, seals, skates, amulets and combs. The excavation also made it possible to produce a reconstruction of the original appearance of the hillfort.
7. Brandenburg an der Havel

Another important hillfort of the Hevelli was Brandenburg an der Havel, which stood in the 8th to 10th centuries and in 928 was surrounded by the German king Henry I. Brandenburg was the seat hillfort of the Hevellian princes. Around 1127 it was the seat of Prince Pribislav-Henry, who was the last prince of the Hevelli. When he died in 1150, his wife “Petrissa” gave the hillfort, as well as the whole territory of the Hevelli, to the German margrave Albrecht the Bear. A kinsman of the deceased Pribislav, however, retook the hillfort in 1153 with the help of some of the Hevelli and a Polish army. In 1157 Albrecht the Bear finally won the hillfort back. In 1165 a Christian cathedral was built on the site of the hillfort, which meant the definitive demise of the hillfort.
8. Behren – Lubchin

children.text: Not far from the village of Behren-Lübchin there stood, from the 10th to the 12th century, a massively fortified island hillfort of the Circipani. It is of interest that this is apparently the hillfort mentioned in the written account of Saxo Grammaticus from 1171. The hillfort again had a circular plan and a long wooden bridge led to it. It was entered through a massive wooden tower, to which a road led from the bridge. Around the year 1200 the hillfort was captured, and traces of heavy fighting were found on the remains of the bridge as well. Who the conqueror of the hillfort was has not so far been precisely established. Behren-Lübchin was one of the last Slavic hillforts to resist the pressure of the Germans and of Christianity.
9. Stargrad
The largest Slavic town was the chief town of the Wagri —
Stargrad

, later renamed Oldenburg by the Germans, where the seat of the prince of the Wagri and a sanctuary were located. The Wagri were a West Slavic tribe living in the Middle Ages on the Wagrian peninsula. They were the north-westernmost tribe of the Obotrite confederation. The area of their settlement, which they took over in the 7th century, covered the east of the present-day German federal state of Schleswig-Holstein. The modern German reconstruction of Stargrad is to be found in the architectural museum “
Oldenburger Wallmuseum
